prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the Z2 quantum spin Hall state and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, which established topological insulators as a new class of quantum matter protected by spin-orbit coupling and time-reversal symmetry

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B013, to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. After reading the whole first round I hold it for the reason I gave at the start and for a stronger one. Six of eight files name the identical trio and the other two rank B013 as their first alternative, but I treat that only as a check that nobody found a scientific flaw, since the chair rightly notes that part of the convergence comes from members reading each other's openings. The substance stands on its own. Spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry gives a Z2 invariant, the invariant forces protected edge channels, and the HgTe wells then showed a conductance near 2e^2/h that disappears in wide samples and under gating. That is a falsifiable mechanism tested quantitatively, and roughly eighteen years of transport and photoemission work in many material families have not overturned it. In answer to the chair's question on the 2016 prize, the one sentence I propose is this: the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and integer quantum Hall-type phases that need broken time-reversal symmetry or a magnetic field, whereas this prize recognises a time-reversal-symmetric insulator whose topology comes from spin-orbit coupling in ordinary materials, with a new invariant and a measured edge-state signature. I would accept that as sufficient to treat the two as distinct recognitions.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and I do not think wording removes it. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal told Molenkamp which material and which well width to use, and Zhang's death means the Foundation cannot recognise it. Hasan's 3D ARPES work is a decisive second experimental strand that the trio leaves out. A trio is therefore a defensible allocation, not a complete history, and the committee should say so openly. I also concede two things to the critics. Applications are modest, so the case rests on conceptual reach and not on devices. And my own first-round claim that the 2016 citation did not cover symmetry-protected band topology is a statement of emphasis; the committee must not oversell the novelty and should let the citation carry the distinction.

responses.point: Pearce asks that the citation not say Kane and Mele predicted the HgTe effect, and asks whether the 2016 overlap is a real obstacle or only a matter of wording.
responses.response: You are right, and I have changed my wording because of it. My round-1 citation said the theory predicted the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators in one clause with the HgTe experiment, which could be read as Kane and Mele predicting the HgTe realisation. They predicted the Z2 state, first in graphene, where the gap is far too small to observe; the HgTe quantum-well proposal came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. The new citation therefore credits the prediction of the Z2 quantum spin Hall state and its first observation in HgTe, with no claim about who proposed the material. On the overlap, I think it is a point of wording and not an obstacle, provided the sentence I gave above is used: time-reversal-symmetric, spin-orbit-driven topology in ordinary materials against the 2016 phase transitions and Hall-type phases.

responses.point: Eriksson says he has moved toward the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio but still asks whether a 2D-only scope underrepresents the 3D discovery, and wants the minutes to record that omitting Hasan is an allocation judgment.
responses.response: I agree with recording it as an allocation judgment and I would put that in the minutes myself. On scope, I would not stretch the citation to cover the 3D class. The words 'a new class of quantum matter' in my citation are justified by the 2D state, because the Z2 invariant and protected edges define the class, and the HgTe experiment shows it in a real material. If the citation said 'topological insulators in two and three dimensions', it would assert credit for a branch whose theory (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents) and experiment (Hasan) are not among the three people, and that is the overclaim the chair's question warns about. I would keep the 3D work as a candidate for a separate discussion rather than squeeze it in.

responses.point: Kroll keeps B006 as his preferred prize because of its clean two-name attribution and closed-loop reproducibility, and moves B013 up to his first alternative, while saying B013's allocation problem is more severe than B006's.
responses.response: I accept the criticism of attribution: B006 is cleaner than B013, and I rank it as my second alternative for that reason. I do not accept it as a reason to put B006 ahead. The Katori and Ye case is a precision capability whose strongest consequences, the redefinition of the second and geodesy, are still prospective, as you say yourself, and it follows the 2005 frequency-comb prize on the same measurement theme. The B013 allocation problem is real, but it is an incompleteness of the trio, not an error in it: each of the three named people did what the citation says. If you wanted to make the case for a two-part prize, I would want to know what B006's citation says about discovery beyond record accuracy, since Olsson asked the same and I did not see an answer.

responses.point: Lindroth holds B002 as her preferred prize, treats B013 as the main rival, and argues that the 2016 prize lowers the novelty of a second topological prize compared with a cold-atom prize.
responses.response: I take the novelty point seriously and answered it above. Where we differ is on what is ready to be credited. Your own concern, five credited names for three seats and Jaksch outside the list, is a larger attribution problem than anything in B013, and the Bloch-Greiner-Zoller trio leaves out Esslinger and Cirac, whose Fermi-Hubbard and simulator contributions are not minor. I also think B002 may be better read as several discoveries (the Mott transition, microscopes, Hubbard-model simulation) than as one, which makes a single sharp citation hard. If the committee wanted a second part for cold atoms, I would need the citation to name one discovery, and I do not yet see it.

responses.point: Danielsson supports the same trio and says Kane and Mele are a single theory contribution that cannot honestly be split, and is cautious on B021 until the anyonic braiding evidence is replicated.
responses.response: I agree on both points. Splitting Kane and Mele would credit a founding paper pair unevenly, and your reasoning is stronger than my round-1 argument for keeping Mele. On B021, I accept your caution and have dropped it as an alternative. The shot-noise fractional charge is secure, but the braiding interferometry is a few years old and the committee would be recognising a result before independent groups have confirmed it. I now list B025 and B006 as alternatives instead.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that a trio omitting Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang authors is a defensible but incomplete allocation, and records that judgment in the minutes.
Whether the one-sentence distinction from the 2016 prize persuades members who raised the overlap; my confidence is high on the physics but not on how outside readers will see it.

Whether the citation wording stays accurate about the HgTe observation, since I cannot independently verify from the supplied files how much of the later nonlocal-transport debate bears on the edge-state interpretation.
B025 and B006 as alternatives: I have not checked in detail the priority questions that Olsson (Andrei's STM work) and Kroll (parallel lattice-clock work) raise.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no recorded collaboration with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan or the authors of the alternatives. My Gothenburg environment overlaps with the Chalmers colleagues on the committee, but that bears on B009, which I do not propose, and not on B013. I have no recusal to declare.
